definition: Innate means inborn — present in a person or creature from the start, not learned or acquired later.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word innate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know innate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The border collie's herding is innate: pups who have never seen a flock will circle the ducklings on their first afternoon in the yard.
Ingrained is weaker than innate: an ingrained habit was ground in by years of repetition — deep, but it arrived through living. An innate trait was already there before any living had been done.
Hardwired goes further than innate — an innate gift can still be neglected or trained into new shapes, but hardwired describes behavior fixed in a creature's wiring, beyond changing at all.

Inherent means built into a thing's own nature — and it works for anything: objects, systems, plans. Innate leans toward living beings and the traits they are born with; a bridge has inherent flaws, a foal has innate ones.
Inborn is the plain twin: present from birth. It's the everyday word where innate is the slightly formal one — but both insist the trait arrived with the creature, not after.

Her brother spent a decade of ear-training drills chasing what she was born holding.
Their conservatory teacher shrugged: perfect pitch, she said, is largely innate — either the wiring came with the child or it didn't.
Innate is the word for Amara's ear because the gift was present from the start: no lessons, no drills, no environment to credit.
Her brother's hard-won ear is the perfect contrast — real skill, but acquired, the card's opposite.
Keep the word's direction in mind, too: innate points at what a living creature brings into the world, the talents and temperaments already in the wiring at birth.

Reviewers reach for it to settle nature-versus-nurture arguments, so use it only when "never taught" is actually true.
For objects and systems, this card's inherent is the right tool; and note that calling a skill innate can shade into backhanded praise, quietly erasing the practice behind it.

The hatchery volunteers used to debate how much help the sea-turtle hatchlings needed to find the water.
The answer, the biologist told them, was none.
The pull toward the brightest horizon is innate: a hatchling that has never seen the ocean digs out at night and runs for the glow.
To prove it, she described lab-raised turtles, incubated in windowless rooms, that still oriented to a dim artificial horizon on their first try.
What the volunteers could change was the beach, not the turtle.
Porch lights and neon confuse that compass, so the town dimmed its shoreline for hatching season.
That summer the volunteers counted nine nests, and every scramble ended in the surf.
